client.note: Not an AWS product. Traffic originates outside the account, so there is nothing to name here.

lb.note: ELB is three products. ALB is the HTTP one and the one a web system design means; NLB is layer 4, and the Classic balancer is previous generation.

service.note: The instance a student pictures when they say "a server". ECS, EKS and App Runner all schedule onto the same hardware, so the sizes below are what any of them ultimately buy.

db.note: RDS runs the engine a student already knows, usually PostgreSQL or MySQL. Aurora is the AWS-built alternative and DynamoDB is not relational at all, so neither is the honest default for a box labelled "database". Prices below are PostgreSQL, Single-AZ; Multi-AZ costs more.

cache.note: Prices below are the Redis OSS node-hour rate. Valkey is cheaper and Memcached matches Redis, so the engine choice moves the number. The memory figures are AWS's own and are not round: a cache.r6g.large is published as 13.07 GiB, being what is left for data after the node reserves its own.

queue.note: A queue one consumer drains. Kafka-style fan-out to many independent readers is a different shape and belongs on the stream broker.

worker.note: A worker is a server that reads from a queue instead of from a socket, so it is the same EC2 hardware as a service. Sizes are shared with `service` rather than repeated, because repeating them would let the two drift.

timeseriesdb.note: Timestream now covers time series through managed InfluxDB, which is also the engine a student is most likely to have met.

coldstorage.note: A storage class of S3 rather than a separate service, chosen because the retrieval delay is the thing being taught.

vectordb.note: AWS sells no standalone vector database. The nearest purpose-built thing is a vector search collection on OpenSearch Serverless, which is also what Bedrock knowledge bases default to.

streambroker.note: Kinesis is the AWS-native one and shows the shard model plainly. Amazon MSK is the choice if the lesson depends on Kafka itself rather than on partitioned streaming.

pubsub.note: Fan-out to subscribers, as against SQS, which is one queue drained by one consumer group. The pair is usually taught together.

websocket.note: A distinct API type from the REST and HTTP ones, because it holds the connection open and bills per connection-minute.

apigateway.note: The HTTP API is the cheaper and simpler of the two request/response types; the REST API is the one with the fuller feature set.

cron.note: The current scheduling product. EventBridge rules on a schedule expression still work and are what older material shows.

ratelimiter.note: Two different products limit rate. WAF drops abusive traffic at the edge, which is what a rate limiter in a diagram usually means; API Gateway usage plans throttle a known caller to a quota.

replica.note: Not a separate product. A replica is an RDS instance sized on its own, so the `db` sizes apply.

shard.note: AWS sells no sharding product for RDS. A shard is one more independent RDS instance and the application decides what goes where, which is the point worth teaching.

edgecompute.note: Two options run at the edge. CloudFront Functions is the light one, for header and URL work at the point of presence; Lambda@Edge runs longer and costs more.

transcoder.note: The file-based transcoder, which is the batch "convert this upload" job. MediaLive is the live-stream counterpart. Elastic Transcoder is the previous generation.
